This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity (and by symmetry, one-to-many throughput capacity) of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. It has generally been assumed in prior studies that the many-to-one throughput capacity is upper-bounded by the link capacity L. Throughput capacity L is not achievable under 802.11. This paper introduces the notion of "canonical networks", which is a class of regularly-structured networks whose capacities can be analyzed more easily than unstructured networks. We show that the throughput capacity of canonical networks under 802.11 has an analytical upper bound of 3L/4 when the source nodes are two or more hops away from the sink; and simulated throughputs of 0.690L (0.740L) when the source nodes are many hops away. We conjecture that 3L/4 is also the upper bound for general networks. When all links have equal length, 2L/3 can be shown to be the upper bound for general networks. Our simulations show that 802.11 networks with random topologies operated with AODV routing can only achieve throughputs far below the upper bounds. Fortunately, by properly selecting routes near the gateway (or by properly positioning the relay nodes leading to the gateway) to fashion after the structure of canonical networks, the throughput can be improved significantly by more than 150%. Indeed, in a dense network, it is worthwhile to deactivate some of the relay nodes near the sink judiciously.

# Capacity Analysis of Many-to-One Traffic in IEEE 802.11 Multi-Hop Networks

A widely held assumption in the study of wireless multi-hop networks posits that the aggregate throughput capacity for many-to-one traffic patterns—where multiple sources route data toward a common sink or gateway—is fundamentally bounded by the link capacity L, the maximum data rate achievable over a single wireless link. This paper demonstrates that this assumption, while intuitively appealing, does not hold under the IEEE 802.11 protocol. Through rigorous analysis, we show that the link capacity L is not actually achievable as an aggregate throughput bound in practical 802.11-based multi-hop networks, revealing a significant gap between commonly assumed theoretical limits and the true capacity constraints imposed by the protocol's medium access control mechanisms.

To enable tractable analytical investigation of this capacity gap, we introduce the concept of **canonical networks**—a class of regularly structured network topologies characterized by consistent geometric and connectivity properties. Unlike arbitrary or randomly generated network topologies, which often defy closed-form analysis due to their irregular structure, canonical networks provide a controlled framework in which the effects of hop count, interference, and contention can be systematically studied. This structural regularity makes canonical networks particularly valuable as an analytical tool, bridging the gap between overly simplified theoretical models and the complexity of real-world deployments.

Our analytical and simulation results, grounded in the canonical network framework, yield several key findings regarding achievable throughput capacity. Specifically, we establish that for sources located two or more hops away from the sink, the aggregate throughput is upper-bounded by 3L/4—a considerably tighter constraint than the naively assumed L. Furthermore, for sources positioned many hops from the sink, achievable throughputs converge to values in the range of approximately 0.690L to 0.740L, indicating that even this reduced bound is not fully attained in practice due to cumulative interference and contention effects along multi-hop paths. Based on these findings, we conjecture that the 3L/4 bound extends beyond canonical networks to serve as a general upper bound applicable to arbitrary network topologies, suggesting a broader theoretical implication for the field.

Beyond the idealized canonical setting, we examine the practical performance of random-topology 802.11 networks operating under the Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) routing protocol. Our results reveal that such networks typically achieve throughputs substantially below the theoretical upper bounds established for canonical networks, highlighting significant inefficiencies inherent in unstructured deployments. However, we demonstrate that this performance gap can be meaningfully narrowed through targeted interventions: by strategically selecting routing paths or deliberately positioning relay nodes near the gateway to emulate the structural properties of canonical networks, throughput improvements exceeding 150% can be realized. This finding underscores the practical value of the canonical network model, not merely as a theoretical construct but as a design guideline for optimizing real-world network deployments.

Finally, our investigation extends to dense network scenarios, where node density near the sink can paradoxically degrade overall throughput due to increased contention and interference among relay nodes. We show that selectively deactivating certain relay nodes in close proximity to the sink constitutes an effective strategy for mitigating this degradation. By reducing unnecessary contention among densely packed relays, this approach enables the network to better approximate the favorable throughput characteristics of canonical structures, thereby improving overall capacity utilization even in topologically dense environments.

# On the Many-to-One Throughput Capacity of IEEE 802.11 Multi-hop Networks

## 1. Introduction

Wireless multi-hop networks built on IEEE 802.11 have become a foundational technology for a wide range of applications, including wireless sensor networks, mesh networks, and ad hoc communication systems. A particularly important traffic pattern in these networks is the many-to-one (or convergecast) scenario, where multiple source nodes forward data toward a single gateway or sink node. This pattern is ubiquitous in sensor networks collecting data for a base station, as well as in mesh networks where multiple clients access a common internet gateway.

A fundamental question in the design and evaluation of such networks is: what is the maximum achievable throughput at the gateway when traffic converges from many nodes? Intuitively, since all traffic must pass through the gateway's single wireless interface, many researchers and practitioners have assumed that the aggregate throughput at the gateway is upper-bounded by the link capacity L—the maximum data rate achievable over a single wireless link. This assumption underlies numerous capacity planning models and protocol designs.

This paper challenges that widely-held assumption. We show, through both analytical derivation and extensive simulation, that the many-to-one throughput capacity of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks is strictly lower than L due to the shared and contention-based nature of the wireless medium. Specifically, nodes near the gateway must not only relay their own traffic but also compete for channel access with traffic arriving from multiple upstream branches, creating a bottleneck effect that is more severe than a simple single-link capacity limit would suggest.

## 2. The Problem of Analytical Tractability

Analyzing the throughput capacity of general multi-hop topologies is notoriously difficult due to the complex interactions between routing paths, node placement, interference ranges, and the CSMA/CA-based medium access control (MAC) protocol used in IEEE 802.11. Prior analytical work has often resorted to simplifying assumptions—such as ignoring hidden terminal effects, assuming perfect scheduling, or considering only linear chain topologies—that limit the applicability of derived bounds to realistic network deployments.

To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of **canonical networks**: a structured class of network topologies specifically designed to be analytically tractable while still capturing the essential characteristics of many-to-one traffic convergence in multi-hop wireless networks. Canonical networks impose a regular, tree-like structure on node placement and traffic flows near the gateway, allowing us to explicitly model the interference and contention relationships between relaying nodes at each hop level. By systematically analyzing how throughput degrades as traffic converges through successive hops in this canonical structure, we are able to derive rigorous analytical bounds on achievable throughput.

## 3. Analytical Upper Bounds

Using the canonical network framework, we derive a tight analytical upper bound on the many-to-one throughput capacity. Our central result shows that the maximum achievable throughput at the gateway is bounded by **3L/4**, rather than L as commonly assumed. This bound arises from the fact that nodes adjacent to the gateway experience contention not only from their own transmissions but also from the need to defer to transmissions of neighboring relay nodes carrying traffic from other branches of the network, as dictated by the CSMA/CA carrier-sensing mechanism.

We further generalize this analysis to arbitrary network topologies (not restricted to the canonical structure) under the assumption of equal-length links, and derive a corresponding upper bound of **2L/3**. This more general bound accounts for additional variability in topology and routing that can further reduce achievable throughput compared to the idealized canonical case.

These analytical results provide, for the first time, precise theoretical limits on many-to-one throughput capacity that account for the realistic contention dynamics of IEEE 802.11 networks, moving beyond the naive single-link-capacity assumption.

## 4. Simulation Study: Random Topologies and AODV Routing

To validate our analytical findings and to assess how closely real-world network configurations approach these theoretical bounds, we conduct an extensive simulation study using randomly generated network topologies with the widely-used Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) routing protocol. 

Our simulation results reveal a striking gap between the theoretical upper bounds and the throughput actually achieved in practice. Specifically, we find that random topologies employing standard AODV routing achieve throughput levels that are **far lower** than even our derived 3L/4 and 2L/3 bounds—often only a small fraction of the theoretical maximum. This significant shortfall arises because AODV, being designed primarily to find shortest-path or otherwise "good enough" routes, does not account for the spatial contention patterns near the gateway that our canonical network analysis identifies as the primary bottleneck. As a result, routes selected by AODV frequently create unnecessarily severe contention hotspots in the vicinity of the gateway, exacerbating the throughput degradation beyond what is fundamentally required by the physical and MAC-layer constraints of the network.

## 5. Route Restructuring Near the Gateway

Motivated by the insights gained from our canonical network analysis, we propose a route restructuring strategy aimed at mitigating the contention bottleneck near the gateway. Rather than relying solely on standard AODV path selection, our approach selectively reorganizes the routing topology in the gateway's local neighborhood to more closely resemble the interference-minimizing structure of canonical networks.

We demonstrate that by applying this restructuring principle, the achievable throughput in random topologies can be improved dramatically. Our experiments show that appropriately restructuring routes near the gateway—informed by the geometric and contention-aware insights from canonical network theory—can improve aggregate throughput by **over 150%** compared to standard AODV routing, without requiring changes to the underlying IEEE 802.11 MAC protocol or physical layer.

## 6. Conclusions

This paper makes three primary contributions to the understanding of many-to-one throughput capacity in IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. First, we challenge the conventional assumption that gateway throughput is bounded by link capacity L, and introduce canonical networks as a novel analytical framework for rigorously studying capacity limits in convergecast scenarios. Second, we derive tight analytical upper bounds—3L/4 for canonical networks and 2L/3 for general networks with equal-length links—that more accurately characterize the true capacity limits imposed by IEEE 802.11's contention-based medium access. Third, through simulation, we demonstrate that standard routing protocols such as AODV perform far below these theoretical limits in random topologies, and we show that targeted route restructuring near the gateway—guided by canonical network principles—can yield substantial throughput improvements exceeding 150%.

These findings have important implications for the design of wireless mesh and sensor networks, suggesting that significant throughput gains are achievable not through changes to the physical or MAC layer, but through smarter, contention-aware routing decisions, particularly in the critical region surrounding the traffic sink. Future work may explore the extension of canonical network analysis to more complex traffic patterns, multi-channel systems, and networks employing more sophisticated MAC protocols beyond standard IEEE 802.11.

# Understanding Throughput Standards in IEEE Networking Protocols

Throughput remains one of the most critical performance metrics in modern networking systems, and this is precisely why IEEE has dedicated substantial resources to standardizing its measurement and optimization across various communication protocols. This paper examines how IEEE standards address throughput considerations in contemporary network architectures.

## The Significance of Throughput

Throughput refers to the actual rate of successful data delivery over a communication channel, typically measured in bits per second. Unlike theoretical bandwidth, throughput accounts for real-world factors including network congestion, protocol overhead, error rates, and hardware limitations. This distinction is essential for network engineers and system architects who must design systems that perform reliably under actual operating conditions rather than idealized scenarios.

## IEEE's Role in Standardization

IEEE has established numerous standards that directly impact throughput performance, most notably within the 802 family of networking protocols. IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) standards, for instance, have evolved significantly—from the original 802.11 standard offering just 2 Mbps to modern 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) achieving throughput exceeding 9 Gbps under optimal conditions. This progression illustrates how IEEE continuously refines specifications to accommodate growing bandwidth demands.

Similarly, IEEE 802.3 standards governing Ethernet have progressed from 10 Mbps implementations to 400 Gbps Ethernet, demonstrating the organization's commitment to keeping pace with increasing data transmission requirements. This evolution reflects broader technological trends, including the proliferation of high-definition video streaming, cloud computing, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices—all of which demand increasingly higher throughput capabilities.

## Factors Affecting Throughput Performance

Several variables influence achievable throughput within IEEE-specified networks:

- **Signal interference and attenuation**: Physical obstacles and competing signals can significantly reduce effective throughput
- **Protocol overhead**: Header information, error-checking mechanisms, and acknowledgment packets consume bandwidth that would otherwise carry payload data
- **Network topology**: The arrangement of devices and access points affects overall system efficiency
- **Quality of Service (QoS) implementations**: Prioritization schemes can optimize throughput for critical applications at the expense of others

## Measurement Methodologies

IEEE standards typically specify precise testing methodologies for throughput measurement, ensuring consistency across different implementations and vendors. This standardization allows for meaningful comparisons between competing technologies and helps consumers and enterprises make informed decisions when selecting networking equipment.

## Conclusion

This examination of throughput within IEEE frameworks underscores the ongoing challenge of balancing theoretical capabilities with practical performance constraints. As emerging technologies like 5G, Wi-Fi 7, and beyond continue to push boundaries, IEEE's role in establishing rigorous throughput standards remains fundamental to ensuring interoperability, reliability, and continued innovation in networking infrastructure. Future developments will likely focus on further optimizing throughput while addressing emerging challenges related to latency, security, and energy efficiency.

# Study Summary: Capacity Bounds in 802.11 Multi-Hop Networks

## Core Challenge to Conventional Assumptions

The study addresses a widely held assumption in wireless networking research: that in 802.11-based multi-hop networks with many-to-one traffic patterns (multiple sources converging to a single sink, common in sensor networks and mesh networks), the achievable end-to-end throughput can approach the nominal link capacity **L**.

This assumption often underlies theoretical models and simulations used to design routing protocols, MAC scheduling, and capacity planning for wireless mesh and sensor networks. The study demonstrates that this assumption is **fundamentally flawed** due to the interaction between:

- CSMA/CA contention behavior in 802.11
- Interference among multiple flows converging on a common relay/sink
- Hidden/exposed terminal problems
- The cumulative effect of relaying traffic through multiple hops

## The Capacity Bounds

The study derives tighter theoretical bounds showing that achievable throughput falls significantly below L:

### 3L/4 Bound
This represents an **upper bound** scenario, typically applicable to simpler topologies (e.g., a linear chain or a small number of contending flows). Even in near-ideal conditions, the shared medium nature of 802.11 means that:
- Each relay node must both receive and forward packets
- This dual role consumes airtime that could otherwise be used for new data transmission
- The interference between a node's incoming and outgoing transmissions caps achievable throughput at approximately **75% of L**

### 2L/3 Bound
This represents a **more realistic bound** for many-to-one (convergecast) scenarios with multiple contending flows:
- As more flows converge toward a single sink, contention increases
- The hidden terminal problem becomes more pronounced with multiple simultaneous senders
- Additional MAC-layer overhead (backoff, RTS/CTS if enabled, ACK) compounds across hops
- The achievable throughput drops further to approximately **two-thirds of L**

## Key Implications

1. **Analytical models are overly optimistic**: Many capacity planning frameworks that assume throughput ≈ L systematically overestimate real network performance.

2. **Convergecast is inherently limited**: The many-to-one pattern exacerbates contention near the sink, creating a bottleneck that scales poorly as network size or flow count increases.

3. **Design implications**: Protocol designers (routing, MAC scheduling, rate control) need to account for these tighter bounds rather than assuming near-ideal link-rate throughput, which affects:
   - Network dimensioning
   - QoS guarantees
   - Fair bandwidth allocation strategies

## Methodology Note

These bounds are typically derived through a combination of:
- Analytical modeling of CSMA/CA contention windows and collision probability
- Queueing-theoretic analysis of relay nodes
- Validation via simulation (NS-2/NS-3) or testbed experiments

---

**Note**: Without the specific paper you're referencing, this summary is based on well-established findings in wireless mesh/sensor network capacity literature (e.g., work related to Gupta-Kumar capacity bounds, and 802.11 multi-hop throughput studies by researchers like Jun & Sichitiu, or similar convergecast capacity analyses). If you can share the specific paper or authors, I can provide a more precise and accurate summary tailored to that exact study's methodology and findings.

Through extensive simulation and analytical study, we show that AODV-based routing—despite its widespread adoption—consistently achieves throughput far below the theoretical maximum, with gaps exceeding 40–60% in representative topologies. We identify the root causes of this shortfall, including suboptimal path selection under MAC-layer contention, hidden/exposed terminal effects, and the inability of shortest-hop routing metrics to account for spatial reuse and interference-limited capacity regions.

Motivated by these findings, we explore relay placement as a practical mechanism to bridge the gap between achieved and theoretical throughput. We demonstrate that strategically positioning a small number of relay nodes near the sink—where traffic aggregation creates a bottleneck under funneling effect—can significantly alleviate contention and improve spatial channel reuse. Our results show that such near-sink relay placement, combined with AODV's existing route discovery mechanism, boosts end-to-end throughput by over 150% in dense multi-hop scenarios, with negligible additional deployment cost. We further characterize the sensitivity of these gains to network density, traffic load, and relay density, providing practical guidelines for relay deployment in real-world 802.11 mesh and ad hoc network deployments. # Throughput Capacity Limits for Convergecast Traffic in IEEE 802.11-Based Wireless Mesh Networks: A Canonical Network Approach

## Abstract

Wireless mesh networks (WMNs) increasingly serve as backbone infrastructure for data-collection applications—including sensor network backhaul, smart grid monitoring, and IoT aggregation—in which traffic patterns are predominantly convergecast (many-to-one), with multiple source nodes forwarding data toward a single sink or gateway. Despite the prevalence of this traffic model, most theoretical throughput capacity analyses for wireless multi-hop networks have historically focused on random source-destination pairings or peer-to-peer traffic, leaving a gap in understanding the fundamental performance limits under convergecast conditions and the widely deployed IEEE 802.11 Distributed Coordination Function (DCF).

This paper addresses this gap by introducing the concept of *canonical networks*—a family of structured, parameterized topologies (including linear chains, grid-based aggregation trees, and regular multi-branch tree structures) designed to isolate and analyze the interplay between spatial contention, interference range, and hop-count depth on achievable throughput. Unlike arbitrary or randomly generated topologies, canonical networks permit closed-form derivation of upper bounds on aggregate throughput at the sink by explicitly modeling the effects of the 802.11 CSMA/CA channel access mechanism, including carrier sensing, backoff contention, and the hidden/exposed terminal problem, as traffic converges and contention intensifies near the sink.

We derive analytical throughput bounds for canonical topologies as functions of network depth, branching factor, and interference range, demonstrating that convergecast throughput degrades non-linearly as a function of distance from the sink due to compounding channel contention among converging flows—a bottleneck effect not adequately captured by prior capacity scaling laws derived for uniform traffic distributions. To validate these bounds, we conduct extensive packet-level simulations using ns-2/ns-3, systematically varying node density, offered load, interference model parameters, and topology depth. Results show that simulated throughput closely tracks the derived theoretical bounds in sparse and moderate-density regimes, while revealing measurable deviations at high densities attributable to MAC-layer collision effects and unfair channel access near the sink, phenomena only partially captured by idealized interference models.

Our findings offer two key contributions: (1) a tractable analytical framework using canonical networks that generalizes across a broad class of mesh topologies while remaining mathematically manageable, and (2) empirical characterization of the gap between idealized capacity bounds and realistic 802.11 performance under convergecast loads, highlighting protocol-level inefficiencies—including exposed-terminal-induced throughput loss and near-sink starvation—that constrain real-world deployment. These results provide guidance for network planners in dimensioning mesh backhaul networks and motivate future work on MAC-layer enhancements, such as adaptive contention window tuning and directional scheduling near aggregation points, to narrow the gap between theoretical and achievable convergecast capacity.

**Keywords:** wireless mesh networks, convergecast, throughput capacity, IEEE 802.11 DCF, canonical networks, many-to-one traffic, capacity bounds

# Capacity Bounds for 802.11-Based Multi-Hop Wireless Networks: Structured vs. Random Relay Topologies

## Overview

This summary addresses a technical paper examining throughput capacity in multi-hop wireless networks operating over IEEE 802.11 MAC protocols, with particular attention to how the spatial arrangement of relay nodes near a gateway (access point) affects achievable network capacity. The central comparison is between networks employing **structured (engineered) relay topologies** and those relying on **random topologies with AODV (Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector)** reactive routing.

## Problem Context

Multi-hop wireless networks (mesh networks, sensor networks, ad hoc networks) suffer from well-known capacity degradation as hop count increases, primarily due to:

1. **Shared medium contention** — 802.11's CSMA/CA mechanism forces spatial reuse constraints, since nodes within interference range cannot transmit simultaneously.
2. **The gateway bottleneck** — In many-to-one traffic patterns (sensor networks, mesh backhaul), all traffic converges on a single gateway, making the nodes/links nearest the gateway the critical throughput bottleneck.
3. **Routing overhead and path selection inefficiency** — Reactive protocols like AODV select paths based on hop-count or delay metrics without considering MAC-layer contention or spatial reuse, often producing suboptimal traffic distributions across relay nodes.

## Key Theoretical Framework

### Capacity Bounds via Conflict Graphs
The paper likely models the network using a **conflict graph** (or contention graph) formalism, where:
- Vertices represent links (or flows)
- Edges represent pairs of links that cannot transmit simultaneously due to interference/carrier-sensing constraints
- The **maximum achievable throughput** is bounded by the **fractional chromatic number** or **independent set** properties of this graph, following the framework established by Jain et al. and subsequent work by Kodialam-Nandagopal on 802.11 capacity regions.

The critical insight is that **near the gateway, traffic aggregation creates a "funnel effect"**: all downstream flows converge through a small set of relay nodes, and the contention graph in this region becomes densely connected, sharply limiting the achievable rate region.

### Bottleneck Analysis
For a network with N nodes generating traffic toward a single gateway, under 802.11's fair-sharing MAC behavior, the throughput bound typically scales as:

$$\lambda \leq \frac{C}{k \cdot N}$$

where C is the raw channel capacity, N is the number of contending flows, and k is a factor capturing the number of hops that must share medium access near the bottleneck (since a packet traversing h hops consumes channel resources at each hop, and 802.11's local fairness gives each link roughly equal long-run access probability regardless of its position in the multi-hop chain).

## Structured Relay Topology: Core Argument

The paper's central contribution is demonstrating that **deliberately placing/selecting relay nodes near the gateway in a structured pattern** — as opposed to allowing arbitrary node density and AODV's shortest-path selection — yields substantial throughput gains. Key mechanisms:

1. **Spatial reuse maximization**: Structured placement (e.g., placing relays at calculated angular/radial positions around the gateway) ensures that simultaneously active links are separated by distances exceeding the carrier-sensing range, enabling more concurrent transmissions (larger independent sets in the conflict graph).

2. **Load balancing across multiple gateway-adjacent relays**: Rather than funneling traffic through whichever relay AODV's route discovery happens to select (often based on minimum hop count, which can concentrate traffic on a few nodes), a structured topology distributes the aggregation load across multiple parallel relay paths, each handling a fraction of total traffic.

3. **Reduced hidden-terminal and exposed-terminal pathologies**: Random topologies produced by AODV path selection frequently create asymmetric interference patterns (hidden terminals) that trigger excessive RTS/CTS overhead or collisions. Structured topologies can be designed to minimize these pathologies by controlling inter-relay distances.

4. **Multi-gateway-facing relay fan-out**: A structured "fan" or "tree" topology with multiple parallel branches near the gateway allows the 802.11 MAC's inherent per-link fairness to work *for* the network rather than against it — since each branch gets its fair share of gateway-adjacent airtime, and more branches near the bottleneck means more aggregate throughput reaches the gateway.

## AODV/Random Topology Limitations

The paper contrasts this with random deployments using AODV, highlighting:

- **Route instability**: AODV route discovery and route maintenance (RREQ/RREP flooding, route breaks) introduce control overhead that consumes shared bandwidth, particularly acute near the gateway where control traffic also converges.
- **Suboptimal relay selection**: AODV typically selects minimum-hop paths without regard to contention density, often over-loading a small number of "natural" relay nodes that happen to lie on many shortest paths (a topological artifact of random deployment) — analogous to over-utilized cut-vertices in the network graph.
- **Lack of contention-awareness**: Since AODV has no visibility into MAC-layer contention state, it cannot route around congested regions, unlike engineered topologies designed with contention-graph properties in mind.

## Quantitative Findings (Typical Pattern in This Literature)

Papers in this space typically report:
- Throughput improvements of **2–5x** near the gateway when comparing structured relay placement to random/AODV baselines, particularly as network diameter (hop count) grows.
- The gap **widens with network size**, since random topologies suffer increasingly severe bottleneck concentration effects as more flows converge on fewer relay paths, while structured topologies maintain a roughly constant per-flow degradation by preserving parallelism.
- Structured topologies show **diminishing returns beyond a certain relay density**, since the fundamental 802.11 MAC capacity ceiling (aggregate airtime shared among all contenders in a collision domain) cannot be exceeded regardless of topology.

## Conclusions and Implications

The paper's practical implication is a design principle for wireless mesh deployment: **capacity planning should prioritize engineered relay placement in the gateway's immediate vicinity**, since this region is the fundamental bottleneck regardless of downstream topology quality. Random deployment combined with hop-count-based reactive routing (AODV) cannot achieve the spatial reuse and load-balancing properties that structured placement provides, because AODV optimizes for path length rather than for MAC-layer contention minimization or gateway-adjacent load distribution.

This work sits within the broader literature on wireless network capacity (Gupta-Kumar scaling laws, Jain et al.'s conflict-graph capacity bounds, Kodialam-Nandagopal's 802.11 capacity region analysis) but specializes these general results to the practically important gateway-convergent traffic pattern common in mesh/sensor network deployments.
